# Key Figures and Factions
Major Historical and Contemporary Figures

Lyjousturnur the Garnet Dragon Lyjousturnur is among the most celebrated heroes on the continent—the dragon who defeated the Nameless Terror when every other force had failed, and whose intervention at the Second Hornhold around 3E 1580 prevented the catastrophe from consuming the last major population center in the northwest. His name is known in courts and taverns from the Smarana coast to the ruins of the northeastern kingdoms. Songs about the battle circulate in at least four languages. The reality of the hero in residence is somewhat different. Visitors to the Concordat expecting a warrior-king holding court in splendor will find instead a sovereign whom the uninformed describe as "reclusive" and whom those closer to the court more diplomatically characterize as "requiring ample sleep." Lyjousturnur is a young male white dragon distinguished by thick, lustrous white scales adorned with unique red crystal growths that give him the appearance of a living mineral masterpiece. His eyes—striking blue with golden sun-like pupils—testify to his divine lineage as a scion of the dragon god Helixus. A pale red mane cascades from his forehead to his neck, while golden claws and large muscular wings complete his imposing physique. The crystalline structures adorning his tail have become iconic symbols throughout the Concordat. He possesses shapeshifting ability, taking the form of a tall, powerful dragonborn that retains his draconic head while adopting a humanoid body covered in scales. This form mirrors his draconic appearance while allowing more convenient interaction in urban settings. He arrived in the Dragontooth Region around 3E 1570, initially establishing himself at Ly's Peak. His decisive victory against the Nameless Terror cemented his reputation as a protector rather than a conqueror. He formally claimed the title of Prince of Dragontooth, recognized by the Second Auromere Empire on the basis of the ancient dragon-mortal covenant tradition and the practical realities of a shattered continent. As a ruler, Lyjousturnur is genuinely ambitious in vision and genuinely indolent in execution. His grand proposals—the mage tower, trade route expansions, diplomatic overtures to foreign powers—are real, but the pace of implementation is constrained by his evident distaste for administrative detail. He establishes sweeping frameworks and lets others fill in the particulars. This temperament proved unexpectedly compatible with the distributed authority model that his Mage Association advisors helped design: a dragon who sleeps through most governance decisions is, paradoxically, the ideal sovereign for a polity that needs its ruler to refrain from governing. What unsettles neighboring monarchs and visiting dignitaries is not his laziness but his education. Lyjousturnur speaks the language of political theory and institutional design with a fluency that betrays sustained engagement with the Mage Association's intellectual tradition. His conversations with advisors extend well beyond elemental magic into questions of representation, jurisdictional architecture, and the structural conditions for stable multi-ethnic governance. A dragon who hoards gold is predictable; a dragon who reads political philosophy is not. His draconic nature remains evident in other respects: intense lust for treasure, volatile temperament when roused, and overweening pride. Regarding the "carnal desires" stereotypically associated with dragons, Lyjousturnur appears to be an exception—at least where the humanoid races of his domain are concerned. No reliable records indicate the Dragon Lord has ever shown such interest in humans, elves, or other bipedal sapient species. Southern bards hoping for tales of "dragon abducts princess" invariably leave the Concordat disappointed. His appetites run elsewhere. Fishermen working the waters west of Garnetport have on more than one occasion witnessed the Dragon Lord on Whalebones Isle—the rocky islet where he habitually feeds after hunting in the Marglus Sea—in the company of sirens, the pair of them slick with blood and offal among the remains of a fresh kill, engaged in congress that no ballad has yet found a tasteful way to describe. The sirens of Whalebones Isle are extremely dangerous to passing vessels, and the Dragon Lord's evident fondness for them has made the islet a permanent exclusion zone in Garnetport's harbour charts. Sailors who have complained about the inconvenience of routing around the isle have been informed, with varying degrees of diplomatic tact, that the Dragon Lord's personal life is not subject to parliamentary review. However, the orcish communities around Larna's Tears Lake and certain southern lordships occasionally report unusual crocodiles in the deep swamps—specimens of extraordinary size with scales of uncommon pallid coloration, some possessing eyes of a disturbingly familiar hue. These reports have never been officially confirmed, and anyone attempting thorough investigation finds themselves politely but firmly "advised" by the Concordat Rangers to explore elsewhere. The Dragon Lord has never commented on the matter. He maintains enthusiastic pursuit of magical knowledge, particularly combat applications, and still personally engages when hunting formidable prey—which, in his case, means the great sea serpents of the Wyrmgale Sea and the whales of both the Wyrmgale and the Marglus. A dragon of his size cannot be sustained by terrestrial game; the mountains offer nothing large enough to constitute a meal, and the logistics of consuming sufficient deer or elk to fuel a body sixty feet long would strip the forests bare within a season. The ocean is the only viable larder. Lyjousturnur hunts roughly twice per week, departing Ly's Rest in the early hours and returning by midday with his kill. From the northern coast he takes sea serpents—solitary predators that grow to lengths rivaling his own and fight with genuine ferocity. From the Marglus to the west he takes whales, which offer less sport but greater caloric yield. The regularity of these flights has made them a background feature of Concordat life: fishing villages along the northern coast set their schedules by the dragon's shadow, and Garnetport dockworkers glancing skyward to see the Dragon Lord hauling a dead whale overhead barely interrupt their conversations. For foreign visitors, the sight remains profoundly disorienting. The surplus from these hunts—smoked, salted, and cured by the kobold household staff at Ly's Seat—furnishes the Dragon Lord's table when receiving guests. Visiting dignitaries dining at Ly's Seat are served sea serpent steaks and whale cuts that the sovereign killed personally; the diplomatic subtext is not subtle, and is not intended to be. Two centuries of twice-weekly hunting have left visible marks on the landscape. Whalebones Isle, a rocky islet off the Marglus coast west of Garnetport, serves as his primary feeding perch for western hunts; its surface is now a topography of layered cetacean skeletons, the oldest calcite-white and crumbling, the newest still strung with drying sinew. The Alchemist's Isle, a comparable formation off the northern Wyrmgale coast, accumulates the remains of sea serpents—and draws rather more scholarly interest, as sea serpent scales are a prized alchemical reagent that commands extraordinary prices in Hornhold's apothecaries and on the continental market. The Dragon Lord has no objection to scavengers collecting what he discards, but reaching either island requires crossing waters that are dangerous in their own right, and the company one finds on arrival is not always welcoming. An incidental consequence of these hunts is that Concordat waters are measurably safer than comparable stretches of coastline elsewhere on the continent. The great sea serpents of the Wyrmgale—apex predators capable of capsizing merchant vessels—have been systematically culled in the waters nearest the Dragontooth coast for over two hundred years. Garnetport's maritime insurance rates reflect this: underwriters charge less for voyages terminating at Garnetport than for equivalent distances to ports further east along the Wyrmgale, a differential that owes nothing to Garnetport's harbour infrastructure and everything to the fact that the local apex predator has a larger apex predator eating it. His two published works—《Magic for Dummys》 and 《Advanced Topics on Elemental Magic》—occupy a peculiar position in continental literary culture. In Garnetport and many jurisdictions across the western continent, both books are banned on the grounds that encouraging unsupervised magical experimentation is recklessly dangerous. In territories where they are not prohibited, they have been among the best-selling magical texts since their publication after 3E 1700—accessible, practical, and written with the cheerful confidence of someone who has never personally worried about a spell going wrong because he is functionally indestructible. The irony that the Concordat's own sovereign is the author of books banned in the Concordat's own capital is not lost on anyone, least of all Lyjousturnur, who appears to find it amusing. The Concordat's national defense relies heavily on Lyjousturnur's personal power and presence, as there is no unified standing army beyond regional guards and the Hornhold Legion. This creates a structural dependency where distributed governance operates under the ultimate guarantee of draconic protection.

The Matter of Ambercrown Lyjousturnur's clutch brother Vignitious departed the continent sometime in the 3E 1560s—before Lyjousturnur's own arrival—leaving Ambercrown without draconic governance. When asked whether he intends to claim lordship over Ambercrown as well, Lyjousturnur has consistently refused. This refusal has produced Ambercrown's distinctive and somewhat awkward geopolitical status: a territory that belongs to no nation and no political entity, governed by local arrangements in the absence of any higher authority willing to assert sovereignty. The situation persists because no continental power is strong enough to claim Ambercrown over the potential objection of the only dragon on the continent, and the only dragon on the continent has declined to claim it himself.

Exodia the Founder A refugee leader who arrived on the Dragontooth coastline approximately 3E 1570–1580, leading a group of displaced persons fleeing the cascading devastation of the Nameless Terror and its aftermath. Her precise origins are unclear—the refugee populations of this period came from so many shattered communities across the continent that individual provenance was often lost in transit—and Exodia herself appears to have considered the question irrelevant. What mattered was what came next, not what had been left behind. Her most significant historical contribution was the pact she negotiated directly with Lyjousturnur. The details remain partially obscured by legend, but its visible consequence was unmistakable: the persistent grey fog that had shrouded the Dragontooth coastline for over two millennia dissipated, rendering the Garnet Coast habitable for the first time since the double-demon invasion of 2E 200. What began as a refugee encampment under Exodia's leadership grew into the city of Garnetport. Her diplomatic skill, courage in directly negotiating with a dragon, and vision for a new society earned tremendous respect among the settlers. Following her death, this respect transformed into veneration, and over generations she was deified as the founder of Garnetport. Today, temples dedicated to Exodia serve as public halls where citizens gather to discuss civic matters, reflecting the democratic aspects of the governance she championed during her lifetime. Annual celebrations of the city's founding include reenactments of her legendary meeting with Lyjousturnur. Her principles continue to influence Garnetport's political culture: the democratic elements of the city's governance are attributed to her vision, her diplomatic approach established the template for human-dragon relations, and her name is invoked in oaths of office and legal proceedings.

The Necromancer of Garnetport Though his name has been deliberately struck from official records, the "Necromancer of Garnetport" remains a cautionary figure in the region's history. An orphaned elven boy raised in Garnetport and educated at the city's original magic academy, he showed exceptional talent before secretly delving into forbidden magics. Around 3E 1680, his experiments caused catastrophic damage to significant portions of Garnetport before he fled. After leaving Dragontooth, his influence expanded dramatically. His dark cult—the Cult of Bones—spread throughout the eastern regions of the continent, with its reach extending as far as the Lothric corridor. The cult's necromantic practices terrorized multiple kingdoms, establishing the Necromancer as one of the most feared figures of his era. Numerous legends surround his ultimate fate. The most persistent tale speaks of a "black castle visible only at night" constructed through necromantic magic as his final stronghold. The Continental Mage Association, Concordat government, and other official organizations have all declared him dead, citing the cessation of cult activity and the passage of sufficient time. Whether he still lives—potentially through unnatural means—remains a subject of frightened speculation.

Magister Thaddeus Ledger A specialized tax collector from approximately 3E 1720 who gained fame for developing the complex taxation system that still serves the Concordat. His meticulous records and fair-minded approach to assessment earned respect even from those paying substantial sums. The annual "Ledger's Day" marking the start of the tax collection season includes ceremonial displays of his original accounting tools, and his methodologies remain foundational to Concordat fiscal administration.

Admiral Lysandra Stormwind The architect of Garnetport's navy around 3E 1650, Admiral Stormwind transformed a small collection of fishing and trading vessels into a formidable maritime force. Her innovative naval tactics and ship designs continue to influence maritime strategy. The flagship of Garnetport's fleet still bears her name. Her contributions were particularly crucial during the Shimmerbay Calamity, when organized naval response proved essential to evacuating survivors and maintaining order.

Chief Scratchscale The first kobold chieftain to pledge allegiance to Lyjousturnur upon the dragon's arrival around 3E 1570. Chief Scratchscale helped rally other kobold tribes to the dragon lord's banner, establishing the foundation for kobold integration into the emerging Concordat structure. His descendants continue to hold prominent positions within kobold society, and the Scratchscale lineage maintains particular influence in Ly's Peak mining operations and religious observances.

Ritual Master Vagnius Galainor A Ritual Master of the Continental Mage Association—a title conferred upon branch leaders, ranking just below Archmage—Vagnius Galainor was a capable southern human mage specializing in summoning and transmutation magic. He stands as one of the foundational figures in magical thermodynamics theory. Around 3E 1000, Galainor disappeared in the forests at the northwestern foot of the Rolthark Range, which have since been known as Mage's Fall Woods. His surviving records consist of several letters explaining his intention to research orcish culture and magic practices in the marsh communities around Larna's Tears Lake. However, the Association's subsequent investigation concluded he had vanished in forests far east of his stated destination. No one knows what occurred. Most peculiarly, Mage's Fall Woods has been, since ancient times, among the most tame and peaceful forests in the entire Concordat—an anomaly that has puzzled scholars for centuries. Some speculate Galainor's final magic created this peace; others suggest his disappearance removed some threat; the more superstitious claim he remains present in some transformed state, maintaining the forest's tranquility.
Major Factions and Organizations

Hornhold Legion The Hornhold Legion represents what is nominally the Concordat's only standing professional military force, though its capabilities have severely atrophied in the era of draconic peace. Born from minotaur military traditions stretching back to the earliest Hornhold iterations, the Legion has undergone significant transformation since Lyjousturnur's arrival. With the dragon's presence providing ultimate security against external threats, the Legion has transitioned from a war-fighting force into what is essentially a constabulary and garrison organization—a shift that causes significant concern among its more traditionalist officers. The four historic legions have been restructured into twelve companies, dispersed across seventeen operational fortresses positioned along the Concordat's trade routes. Rather than training for large-scale warfare, the Legion's primary mission has become patrolling and securing trade routes in coordination with the Concordat Rangers. Legionnaires spend more time escorting merchant caravans and maintaining order at remote outposts than drilling for battle formations. Despite this operational shift, the Legion maintains its historically demanding training standards. A qualified legionnaire must demonstrate proficiency in heavy armor combat with melee weapons and bows, as well as restoration magic, alteration magic, and basic evocation. These requirements reflect the classic minotaur military philosophy that every soldier should be a versatile, self-sufficient warrior rather than a specialist dependent on support. However, this also creates severe and chronic recruitment challenges. Though the Legion abandoned its minotaur-only composition generations ago and now accepts qualified candidates of all species, three of its four legions operate at significantly reduced strength—typically 60–70% of nominal capacity. The combination of demanding requirements, modest compensation relative to commercial opportunities, and reduced perceived necessity has made recruitment increasingly difficult. Force Deployment: Garrison Forces (~4,000 personnel): The bulk of the Legion, permanently assigned to static defense across major border fortresses (3, each ~500 soldiers), medium hub fortresses (5, each ~250), and minor outposts (9, each ~100). Headquarters guard details of ~200 each in New and Old Hornhold City. Patrol & Logistics Corps (~2,000 personnel): Small mobile units patrolling the road network, escorting caravans, and maintaining supply lines. The most publicly visible arm of the Legion, effectively locked into ongoing duties. Strategic Reserve (~1,000 personnel): The Legion's only true mobile reaction force, critically small and itself divided: a Deeproot Quick Reaction Company (~300), a Hornhold Mobile Column (~300), and Ly's Seat Guard (~400, functioning as combined honor guard, engineering corps, and the dragon's personal reserve). The Concordat Rangers A semi-official adventurer organization formally established around 3E 1710 during the formalization of the Concordat. The Rangers' institutional origins are conventionally traced to the dissolution of the Continental Adventurer's Guild during the Continental Decline, and their formal charter reflects the Guild's organizational model. In practice, however, the Rangers also absorbed significant personnel and operational knowledge from the mercenary companies and armed bands that Lyjousturnur disbanded during the early decades of his rule. Many of these organizations had deep roots in the mountain people and Orc communities of the Deeproot region—veterans who knew every trail, smuggling route, and hidden refuge in the territory. Their integration into the Rangers gave the organization a local expertise and decentralized operational culture that a purely top-down institution could never have replicated. While the old Guild operated across multiple kingdoms with centralized authority, the Rangers represent a regional adaptation—closely integrated with Concordat governance while maintaining operational independence. The Rangers' distinctive chapter structure—Garnetport Rangers, Deeproot Wardens, Hornhold Sentinels, Ly's Peak Delvers, and the semi-independent Whisperleaf Wardens—reflects both the Concordat's geographic diversity and the practical reality that the organization's roots lie in multiple distinct local traditions rather than a single institutional ancestor. The Rangers serve dual functions: routine monster hunting, exploration, and protection services, while also functioning as a military reserve that can be mobilized during emergencies. The Ranger Charter contains important exemptions to Garnetport's magical regulations, originally limited to "necessary counter-magical measures" but gradually expanded to include preparation and training. This created a legal grey zone where magical practice was permissible under Ranger supervision—an unofficial training path exploited by many local magical aspirants. However, following intense public pressure during the Mage Tower controversy, the Garnetport city council passed a resolution banning the local chapter from recruiting within city limits, severing this path to magical education for Garnetport's citizens. Lyjousturnur holds the power to override this decision but has thus far chosen not to intervene in the city's internal governance on the matter.

Cont inental Mage Association, Dragontooth Branch Headquarters: Old Hornhold City Leadership: Ritual Master Elinlyia Moonlit (Whisperleaf Elf; Advisor to Lyjousturnur) The Dragontooth branch is, by default, the largest Mage Association presence in the continental northwest—a distinction that reflects the Association's decline rather than the branch's strength. In the era before the Nameless Terror, the Association maintained major installations across the Smarana Plains, the Gem Plateau, and the northeastern territories, with its apex institution, MU Ogustus, operating as the continent's singular center of advanced magical scholarship. That infrastructure is gone. MU Ogustus was destroyed during the Nameless Terror. Its successor, MU Archmages, was established in Lothric in 3E 1525 but itself destroyed during the Year of the Azure Tide in 3E 1564. The current primary educational body—informally known as MU Luckas, after the Sage who sacrificed himself to stop the Necromancer of Garnetport—maintains the ancient admission standards but operates at a fraction of its predecessors' scale. The Smarana Plains kingdoms and the Gem Plateau's successor states have not restored the Association's pre-Terror position. Public attitudes toward organized magic across the western continent have hardened dramatically: the Sea of Gold demonstrated for millennia that concentrated magical power produces tyranny; the Nameless Terror—widely believed by the continental public to have been unleashed by reckless mages on the Lissnen Plains—demonstrated that it can also produce apocalypse. The Association's institutional prestige, once unassailable, has not recovered from the suspicion that the magical establishment bears some responsibility for the worst catastrophe in continental history. In this climate, the western kingdoms' embrace of magical conservatism has left the Association's regional branches diminished, underfunded, and politically marginalized. The Dragontooth branch's relative prominence is therefore a matter of local circumstance rather than continental significance. Hornhold's minotaur military tradition, which requires magical proficiency as a baseline soldier qualification, provides institutional demand for magical education that does not exist elsewhere in the northwest. The branch maintains its headquarters in Old Hornhold City, positioning itself near the Grand Archive's old stacks and the University of Hornhold's Faculty of Magical Studies. Alongside the University, the Association represents the only legally sanctioned magical institution in the Concordat outside the Rangers' limited exemptions. Ritual Master Elinlyia Moonlit holds a unique triple portfolio: branch head, Professor of Transmutation at the University, and personal tutor to Lyjousturnur. She graduated from MU Archmages during its brief existence—one of the few living mages who can claim that distinction. Her influence is paramount in shaping the Concordat's magical policy, balancing the region's post-Terror caution with the practical necessity of regulated magical practice. The Association's deeper significance within the Concordat lies not in its magical capacity but in its political-intellectual role. It was senior Association mages who, in consultation with Lyjousturnur and the Arcane Sage, designed the distributed authority framework that became the Concordat's governance model. The Association's two-millennia tradition of institutional design—the same tradition that produced the Lissnen Plains democracy—provided the intellectual architecture for a polity that needed to accommodate populations from radically different governance traditions. This contribution is not widely advertised; the Association's public profile in the Concordat is that of a scholarly institution, not a political one. But its fingerprints are on the constitutional structure, and its senior members continue to serve as advisors, legal theorists, and archival custodians for the parliament's proceedings.

The Coven An illegal underground organization, The Coven takes its name from the term southern humans originally used to describe the shamanistic gatherings of mountain people communities. Unlike the dismissive stereotype, the Coven is deeply rooted in the traditional practices of mountain people and orcish communities—ancient magical knowledge that predates the Concordat and often conflicts with contemporary regulations. The Coven preserves and practices traditions that official authorities view with alarm: ancient corpse-reanimating rituals that are fundamentally necromantic, though mountain people practitioners insist they serve legitimate cultural purposes; the "Heart Replacement" ceremony, functionally identical to lich transformation but embedded in indigenous elder-preservation rites; magic that disrupts spatial continuity; and shadow magic that stands in direct opposition to divine magical traditions. Due to the Concordat's magical restrictions—particularly Garnetport's severe limitations—a large number of practitioners participate in the Coven's networks out of necessity rather than malicious intent. A gifted human in Garnetport who cannot access approved institutions, a dwarf interested in earth magic traditions not taught at the University, an orc studying ancestral transformation magic—all might connect with the Coven because no legitimate alternative exists. The network functions through personal connections and secretive gatherings, with local chapters varying dramatically in practices and ethical standards. The Coven's preservation of genuinely dangerous traditions—and its occasional harboring of practitioners who engage in forbidden magics—makes complete tolerance impossible. Official policy vacillates between periodic crackdowns and tacit acceptance, creating a persistent cat-and-mouse dynamic. The Mage Tower controversy has intensified this tension: opponents of the tower argue that legitimate magical education would undercut the Coven's recruitment base, while supporters of the restrictions counter that any expansion of magical access risks producing another Necromancer of Garnetport.
# Sites of Interest
The Dragonspire Duo Tower System

Two lighthouse towers, both constructed entirely through Lyjousturnur's draconic magic, form a sophisticated navigational aid for maritime traffic approaching Garnetport. The first tower rises from the small island west of Garnetport, emitting a distinctive red light. Surrounding buildings on the island comprise the Temple of Helixus, making this both a religious site and a navigational landmark. The red beacon serves as the primary approach marker for vessels entering the harbor from the western and southern seas. The second tower crowns the peak of Ly's Peak itself, the highest point in the Dragontooth Mountains, broadcasting a powerful white light visible for extraordinary distances. This elevated position allows the beacon to serve vessels far out at sea. Together, the two light sources enable triangulation navigation—ships can determine their precise position and bearing by measuring the angles between the red and white lights. This system represents one of the most advanced navigational aids in the known world, and its magical construction ensures the lights never fail, burn with perfect consistency, and require no maintenance or fuel.
Wayforts

Scattered throughout the Deeproot region, mysterious standing-stone structures known by mountain people as "wayforts" provide instantaneous teleportation between locations. These stone monuments can transport individuals carrying enchanted items between wayfort nodes, functioning as a limited but functional fast-travel network. The carved styling clearly identifies these as Water People constructions, though their magical principles remain poorly understood even by contemporary scholars. Unfortunately, all surviving wayforts occupy relatively remote locations—those that may have existed in central, heavily trafficked areas have presumably been destroyed or lost over the centuries. This remoteness limits their practical utility for most citizens. Adventurers, hunters, and scholars interested in Water People technology make the most frequent use of the wayfort network, while common travelers find conventional roads more convenient than journeying to distant wayfort sites. The University of Hornhold maintains documentation of all known wayfort locations and periodically sends expeditions to study their function and search for additional nodes.

Dwarven Ruins Beyond Khazdurat and Ghalakdum—the two major ruins that have been extensively explored due to their relatively accessible locations—most large-scale dwarven sites remain in states ranging from "discovered but unexplored" to "completely unknown." Kobold communities typically occupy smaller abandoned dwarven installations, but the scale of the historical Dwarf Kingdom suggests that multiple ruins comparable to Ghalakdum in size likely remain undiscovered in the high mountains. Population estimates from the kingdom's peak period indicate infrastructure far exceeding what has been documented, suggesting vast underground complexes still hidden within the peaks. Both the University of Hornhold and the Continental Mage Association Dragontooth Branch actively purchase information about potential ruin locations and regularly organize expedition teams to investigate promising leads. These expeditions face significant challenges: treacherous mountain terrain, kobold territorial concerns, structural instability in ancient excavations, and occasional hostile creatures that have made ruins their lairs. The potential rewards—lost dwarven knowledge, ancient artifacts, mineral wealth, and historical insights—continue to draw adventurers and scholars despite the risks. The discovery of a major unexplored ruin could represent a career-defining achievement for an archaeologist or a fortune-making opportunity for an adventuring company.

Sunken Garden Along the middle Garnet River, numerous Water People archaeological sites can be found, though most lie beneath water or buried in the silt of ancient river channels. Like the wayforts, a few sites located away from the current riverbanks have survived in better condition. The Sunken Garden represents the most extensive of these preserved sites. Located on the shores of Merian's Mercy lake, southeast of Highpass, the complex is split between water and land: approximately half the structure extends into the lake while the other half is built into the mountainside. This represents typical late-period Water People architecture, showcasing their sophisticated integration of hydraulic engineering and construction. The excavated land portions have yielded tremendous quantities of Water People metal—the distinctive blue-tinted alloy that has never been successfully replicated. Archaeological teams have documented elaborate water management systems, residential spaces, what appear to be ritual chambers, and storage facilities containing remarkably preserved artifacts. The submerged portions remain unexplored, as the combination of murky water, structural instability, and unknown magical wards has prevented comprehensive underwater investigation. Persistent rumors suggest the land sections contain mechanisms or switches that could drain or provide access to the underwater areas, though no expedition has confirmed this. Intriguingly, a map discovered within the Sunken Garden indicates another major site should exist near Lake Aqa, but despite numerous searches, this installation has never been located. Some speculate it may be completely submerged or buried, while others wonder if the map represents plans for a site never completed.

Lost Southern Outposts Of the seventeen fortresses currently operational within the Concordat, nine date from the southern human expansion periods and remain in use—most positioned along the Southern Way through Deeproot's central and southern regions or maintained as private holdings by the southern lords. However, in western Deeproot, numerous abandoned fortresses stand in various states of decay. Most occupy remote locations that have reverted to wilderness, abandoned during the two major withdrawal periods (around 3E 1100 and 3E 1400, when human expansion faltered or retreated). After centuries of neglect, these structures range from picturesque ruins to dangerous, partially collapsed death traps. Some abandoned forts have acquired haunting legends—stories of soldiers who never left their posts, of battles that replay on certain nights, of treasures cursed by those who died defending them. Others have become havens for outlaws: smugglers storing contraband, bandits using defensible positions as bases, Coven practitioners conducting forbidden experiments, and occasionally more dangerous entities like vampires or other undead establishing lairs in structures associated with violence and death. The remote locations and uncertain conditions make these sites attractive to adventurers seeking fortune or challenge, though many expeditions have ended poorly when explorers underestimated the dangers—both natural and supernatural—lurking in these forgotten military installations.

The Black Market of Curiosities A legendary underground market catering to private collectors and smugglers, the Black Market of Curiosities allegedly operates within a hidden section of Deeproot's Underground Market. This clandestine venue trades in items that official markets cannot or will not handle: Water People metal (technically legal with documentation, but the market offers undocumented sales) Singing Crystals (exported from kobold territories in violation of strict regulations) Crystal Heart fragments (illegal under both kobold religious law and Concordat protection of sacred sites) Elven Amber Script (subject to vigorous elven repatriation efforts) Black Garnetport Relics (unregulated but ethically controversial) Various contraband magical items, forbidden texts, and questionable artifacts Authorities have conducted multiple raids attempting to locate and shut down the market, but all efforts have proven futile. Informants provide contradictory information about its location, and any given raid finds only empty chambers or innocent merchants. Some speculate the market operates on a rotating schedule, occupying different spaces within the vast underground network. Others suggest Water People portal magic or similar technologies allow instant evacuation when raids are detected. Despite official denials, the market's existence is widely accepted among collectors, smugglers, and those seeking items unavailable through legitimate channels. The market's apparent invulnerability has become a source of frustration for authorities and a symbol of the limits of government power in the face of determined underground commerce.

Forgotten Sanctum The legendary workshop of the Necromancer of Garnetport supposedly lies hidden within the sewers beneath Garnetport's old quarter (the northeastern section of the Middle City). Though no one has confirmed its location or contents with certainty, the Sanctum exerts powerful attraction on the most ambitious magical practitioners. Rumors suggest the workshop contains: The Necromancer's research notes on forbidden magics Artifacts of terrible power left behind in his hasty flight Necromantic implements and prepared materials Possibly functional defenses or traps protecting his secrets City authorities officially deny the Sanctum's existence, claiming it's a legend perpetuated by those seeking to romanticize a criminal's legacy. However, periodic reports of strange occurrences in specific sewer sections—unexplained lights, unnatural cold, sounds of arcane experimentation—keep the legend alive. The search for the Forgotten Sanctum represents the dark mirror to legitimate archaeological exploration: rather than seeking historical knowledge or lost technology, seekers hunt for power and forbidden secrets. Those obsessed with finding it are precisely the individuals most likely to misuse whatever they discover, creating a situation where authorities cannot acknowledge the Sanctum's existence without encouraging dangerous treasure hunts, yet cannot completely suppress interest in what may be the most significant repository of dark magical knowledge in the Concordat.
#Myths, Legends, and Lost Treasures
Lost Artifacts and Treasures

Kronirr's Sword According to minotaur legend, the Water People girl whom Kronirr rescued from the dark forest gifted him a blade of extraordinary power. The sword is described as gleaming with a soft blue luminescence, never corroding or dulling, capable of cutting through flowing water itself, and possessing the ability to summon storms when wielded by one worthy of its power. The blade disappeared during the upheavals that struck the Second Hornhold in its early centuries. However, correspondence from the later Second Hornhold era—preserved letters dating to around 3E 1000—explicitly mention the sword having been recovered at some point. The letters frustratingly provide no details about who found it, where it was kept, or what became of it subsequently. No one knows the sword's current location. Theories abound: some claim it remains in the private collection of a prominent Archon's family, passed down as a jealously guarded heirloom. Others insist it lies locked in a secret vault within the Grand Archive, too dangerous or politically sensitive to display publicly. More pessimistic scholars believe it was carried away from the Dragontooth Region entirely, perhaps claimed by a foreign dignitary or sold to collectors abroad. The most romantic speculation suggests it rests in Lyjousturnur's personal treasury, either gifted to the dragon or acquired through his extensive hoard collection. The Grand Archive currently displays what it explicitly labels as a replica—a blue-tinted blade crafted to match legendary descriptions, created for educational purposes. Whether this honesty reflects genuine ignorance of the original's location or deliberate misdirection remains unknown.

The Crystal Crown of the Dwarf Kings An eight-pointed star-shaped crown of pure gold, encrusted with gemstones of extraordinary size and quality. According to dwarven records, the crown was fashioned from crystals found in the deepest mines of Ly's Peak and possessed the power to dramatically enhance the magical abilities of its wearer—whether amplifying existing talents or granting magical perception to those without natural gifts. The crown was discovered around 3E 1466 in the depths of Ghalakdum, creating tremendous excitement in archaeological circles. It was brought to Aquilon for public exhibition, where scholars from across the Concordat traveled to study this legendary artifact. However, during the exhibition, the crown disappeared under mysterious circumstances. Subsequently, the crown came into the possession of a lord in southern Deeproot—though how he acquired it was never clearly established. His ownership proved brief and tragic: a series of brutal murders struck those connected to the crown, and in the chaos, the artifact vanished once again. The crown's curse—if curse it be—may have claimed many victims, but it has not destroyed the artifact itself. A fragment believed to be one of the crown's eight points appeared in Deeproot's Black Market around 3E 1755, purchased by an anonymous collector who subsequently donated it to the Mercurian Exchange. The fragment now occupies a place of honor in the Exchange's exhibition hall in Garnetport, displayed in a specially warded case. Analysis confirms it matches descriptions of the crown's construction, though whether the remaining seven points survive—and where they might be—remains unknown.

Water People's Blue Metal Formula The Water People were renowned for their distinctive blue-tinted metal—an alloy that gleams with an inner azure light and shows absolutely no signs of corrosion even after millennia of exposure to water and air. Despite extensive study by metallurgists and alchemists across multiple kingdoms, the manufacturing process remains an unsolved mystery. Contemporary smiths can only work with excavated materials from Water People sites, carefully reshaping existing pieces rather than creating new alloy. Complete weapons or implements in good condition command astronomical prices—a single intact Water People blade might purchase a small estate. Even fragments and damaged pieces are zealously sought, and many adventurers risk the dangers of exploration hoping to discover caches of this legendary material. However, evidence suggests that Ritual Master Vagnius Galainor may have solved the mystery before his disappearance. Prior to his journey to Larkghet around 3E 1000, he sent a small piece of self-manufactured blue metal to his friend in the Grand Archive, accompanied by a letter that has been meticulously preserved: "My dear Lithorinir... I believe I have cracked the mystery of the blue metal. I have conceived of such an elegant solution that it makes my past decade of work seem utterly foolish... This is a sample—please test its properties for me." Analysis of the sample confirmed it possessed properties identical to genuine Water People metal, proving Galainor's claim. Unfortunately, his research materials and notebooks disappeared with him into Mage's Fall Woods. Despite extensive searches of the forest and surrounding areas, no trace of his papers has ever been found. The formula's loss represents one of the Concordat's greatest tragedies of lost knowledge—a breakthrough that could have revolutionized metallurgy and weaponcraft across the continent, vanished with a single man's unexplained disappearance. Occasionally, forgers claim to have rediscovered the formula and offer "new" blue metal for sale, but expert analysis invariably reveals these as frauds using either conventional metals with applied enchantments or, in sophisticated cases, small amounts of genuine Water People metal worked into new forms to deceive buyers.

The Obsidian Relics of Garnetport Since Garnetport's founding around 3E 1600, fishermen and coastal workers have periodically recovered unusual artifacts from the nearby waters. These objects—characterized by their black coloration, fine-polished curves, and distinctive seamless construction—have defied conventional explanation. Locally known as "sea gifts" or "night treasures," they appear in various forms: small figurines, curved implements of unknown purpose, and occasionally jewelry-like items that seem designed for bodies with non-human proportions. Most residents casually dismiss them as cargo from ancient shipwrecks, but several scholars from the University of Garnetport have advanced more controversial theories. Professor Maelis Thornbridge suggests they might predate even the Water People, pointing to construction methods that appear to use no known metallurgical techniques from any documented civilization. The materials themselves resist standard alchemical analysis, showing properties inconsistent with known metals. Testing by university artificers shows the objects absorb and retain heat in patterns that suggest they might once have served magical purposes. Without permission to conduct deeper magical analysis due to Garnetport's restrictions, conclusive identification remains impossible. The Mercurian Exchange maintains a small exhibition of these artifacts, while private collectors quietly pay premium prices for newly discovered specimens despite—or perhaps because of—their mysterious origins.

The Violet Gold Staff A gilt staff bearing a distinctive violet lustre, the Violet Gold Staff is one of the personal relics of Elandorr Sunwhisper, the Sage of Dragon. The staff was crafted in the early Third Era and is, by any conventional measure, a superb spellcasting amplifier: it enhances the wielder's magical output across a broad range of disciplines and responds with particular sensitivity to practitioners of high natural talent. What sets the Violet Gold Staff apart from other legendary implements, however, is its will. The staff chooses its own master. Over some fifteen hundred years of documented history, the staff has served more than five hundred spellcasters—lingering with some for decades, abandoning others after a single use, and on several recorded occasions simply vanishing from a locked vault to reappear in the hands of someone on the other side of the continent. No pattern has been identified in its selections: it has chosen archmages and hedge witches, elves and humans, scholars and soldiers. The only consistent observation is that the staff never stays with anyone permanently.

After 3E 1540, Elandorr transferred the staff to Vignitious the Garnet, the dragon lord of Ambercrown and Lyjousturnur's clutch brother. When Vignitious later departed the continent, the staff remained in Lyjousturnur's keeping for approximately a decade. During this period, both dragons made modifications to the staff's enchantments—an act of considerable audacity, given the artifact's provenance.

Vignitious added a spell now known as "Vig's Elemental Storm," a devastating area-effect incantation that induces violent elemental chaos in the surrounding environment. The spell's design was openly described as being modeled on certain properties of the Nameless Terror—specifically its capacity to destabilize ambient magical fields. This admission provoked widespread alarm across the continent. For a time, the staff was regarded as a forbidden object, and several institutions called for its destruction or permanent sequestration.

Lyjousturnur subsequently added his own variant, "Lyjou's Elemental Storm," built on the same principles but significantly tempered: the necromantic and psychic shock components present in Vignitious's version were stripped out, producing an effect that was still formidable but no longer carried the Terror's most disturbing signatures. The modification did not remove Vig's original spell from the staff—both versions remain accessible to a sufficiently skilled wielder—but Lyjousturnur's addition was widely interpreted as a deliberate corrective, a signal that the staff need not be feared.

Around 3E 1670, the staff appeared in the hands of other practitioners, resuming its ancient pattern of wandering between chosen wielders. Its current location is unknown—as is typical. Today the Violet Gold Staff carries not only the legacy of the Sage of dragon who made it, but also the marks of two dragons who reshaped it: one who saw in the world's worst catastrophe a source of power worth replicating, and one who saw the same catastrophe and chose to file down its edges. Between those two impulses, the staff continues its long journey across the continent, choosing whom it will.
Legendary Figures and Their Legacies

The Wandering Smith A legendary dwarven craftsman who traveled throughout the region after the Dwarf Kingdom's fall, creating extraordinary tools and weapons for communities that showed him kindness. His creations allegedly never break and perform their functions with supernatural efficiency—a Wandering Smith axe that never dulls, a plow that turns soil effortlessly, a hammer that strikes true without fail. Various communities throughout Deeproot and Hornhold claim to possess authentic "Wanderer's Work," though experts believe most are clever forgeries trading on the legend's reputation. Genuine pieces—if any survive—would be virtually impossible to distinguish from exceptionally well-made conventional tools without extensive use over time. The Smith himself vanished from historical record around 3E 900, with the last confirmed sighting placing him in the foothills between Deeproot and the Rolthark Range. Some believe he finally died of age or accident; others romantically suggest he simply walked into the mountains and returned to whatever hidden fastness the last dwarves retreated to when their kingdom fell.

The Mist Walker A legendary figure in Deeproot folklore, particularly associated with the Mist Valleys, described as a being who navigates the dangerous mists with supernatural ease. Tales vary wildly—some portray the Mist Walker as a benevolent guide who rescues lost travelers, while others describe a trickster who leads people astray for unknowable purposes. The Mist Walker appears as a tall, powerfully built figure with distinctly orcish features. Its skin tone shifts with mist density, ranging from deep forest green in thick fog to pale sage in lighter vapor. Amber eyes glow like beacons, visible even through the densest mist. What makes the Mist Walker particularly fascinating is how its appearance has evolved over centuries, mirroring the cultural development of the Dragontooth region: Early Period (~3E 1000–1100): The earliest documented encounters describe traditional orcish marshland attire—leather garments adorned with reptile scales, bone jewelry, and furs. Most distinctive was a headdress resembling a crocodile skull with antlers, matching ceremonial garb worn by marsh orc shamans from southeastern Dragontooth. Transitional Period (~3E 1100–1400): Descriptions shift toward a fusion of orcish and "mountain people" aesthetics—the figure retains orcish physiognomy but wears mixed cultural elements suggesting the blending of populations during this era. Modern Period (~3E 1400–present): Recent sightings describe the Mist Walker in more ambiguous terms, sometimes appearing in clothing that seems Water People in origin, leading to speculation that the entity might be a ghost or transformed remnant of that vanished civilization. Mountain people in remote valleys claim the Mist Walker is actually the ghost of the last Water People king, eternally searching for his lost people through the mists that now cover lands where their cities once stood. This theory has gained traction among scholars studying Water People decline, though empirical evidence remains frustratingly absent.

The Pale Leviathan of the marshland "I'm telling you, the thing was over forty feet long! Covered head to tail in snow-white scales, and its eyes—blue with flecks of gold..." — Marquis Godric Wardell, recounting an encounter in the wetlands near Gramma Stream For generations, scattered reports have emerged from the marshlands surrounding Larna's Tears Lake—particularly the wetlands fed by multiple Streams—describing an enormous reptilian creature unlike any known swamp predator. Witnesses consistently describe a crocodilian of impossible size, distinguished by pale or white scales that seem almost luminescent in the marsh mist, and eyes bearing an unusual blue-gold coloration. The orcish communities of Larkghet interpret these sightings through their traditional theological lens. Local shamans maintain that the creature is a manifestation of Helixus himself—the god appearing in his aspect as "guide at the gate between life and death," watching over the sacred marshlands where so much orcish ancestral history resides. Some elders conduct quiet rituals of offering near reported sighting locations, treating the appearances as divine visitations to be honored rather than investigated. The feudal vassals serving under Marquis Wardell take a decidedly darker view. They insist the creature must be the work of a hag—perhaps one dwelling in the deeper reaches of Mistymarsh who has created or summoned this monstrosity through forbidden magic. Several have petitioned for Concordat Rangers to mount an expedition to locate and destroy whatever witch is responsible. Official investigations into the matter have been notably... unenthusiastic. Ranger patrols in the area report finding no evidence of hag activity, and requests for more thorough searches tend to be quietly buried in administrative proceedings. The creature—if it exists—remains unconfirmed, unexplained, and undisturbed. Those familiar with the Dragon Lord's distinctive coloration have occasionally noted certain similarities, but such observations are generally kept to private conversations and never committed to writing.

The Dragon's Larder: Whalebones Isle and the Alchemist's Isle Every coastal civilization has its sea monster stories. The Concordat's distinction is that its sea monster stories are about the monster that eats the other monsters. Garnetport's fishing fleet has accumulated over two centuries of observations of the Dragon Lord's hunting flights, and these have crystallized into a rich oral tradition that sits somewhere between practical seamanship and epic poetry. The most celebrated accounts describe encounters with great sea serpents—creatures that do not submit to predation quietly. Fishermen who have witnessed these battles at close range describe the sea boiling white as serpent and dragon thrash in the shallows, the crack of reptilian jaws on draconic scale audible over the wind, and the eventual stillness as Lyjousturnur hauls his kill skyward trailing loops of intestine like grotesque pennants. The oldest and most retold of these accounts is "The Storm Serpent Ballad," which describes a hunt during a winter gale in which the Dragon Lord fought a sea serpent of unprecedented size for the better part of an hour before killing it within sight of Garnetport's harbour wall. The ballad is performed in at least three versions—one favoured by Garnetport's dockside taverns, a more polished rendition popular with Auromerian visitors, and a kobold version sung at Ly's Seat that claims to be the most accurate and is certainly the most bloodthirsty. The Sirens of Whalebones Isle Whalebones Isle's siren colony is a subject that Garnetport's polite society prefers to discuss obliquely, if at all. The sirens arrived within the first decade of the Dragon Lord's hunting routine—drawn, presumably, by the reliable supply of carrion—and have never left. Their relationship with Lyjousturnur is not predator-and-prey, not master-and-servant, and not—despite what certain southern romancers have attempted—anything that can be comfortably narrated in a court ballad. Sailors whose routes take them within visual range of the isle on feeding days report scenes that are, by universal consensus, extraordinary and not suitable for the company of the devout. The Dragon Lord's protection of the colony is absolute and unspoken: no formal decree has ever been issued, but the single recorded instance of a Garnetport merchant attempting to "clear" the sirens for a salvage operation on the whale-bone deposits ended when the merchant's petition was returned with a single claw-mark scored across the page. The merchant found alternative investments. The Alchemist's Crossing The northern coast's contribution to Concordat folklore is quieter and stranger. Where the western tales are full of blood and spectacle, the northern stories have the quality of fairy tales—solitary figures undertaking dangerous journeys for precious materials, aided or hindered by forces beyond mortal understanding. The canonical version involves a Hornhold apothecary, usually unnamed, who sets out in a small boat on a storm-dark night to reach the Alchemist's Isle for sea serpent scales needed to save a dying patient. The storm overwhelms the boat; the apothecary is drowning; and then a merfolk appears—sometimes male, sometimes female, depending on the teller—and guides the boat to the island's lee shore. The apothecary fills their satchel with scales. Before departure, the merfolk presses a night-pearl into the apothecary's hand and bestows a kiss that fills the lungs with breathable water. The apothecary returns to Hornhold, saves the patient, and never speaks of what happened until their deathbed. The night-pearl glows on the mantelpiece for years afterward, dimming only when the apothecary dies. Hornhold scholars have documented at least four individuals who claim direct experience of some version of this story—none of whom will discuss it in detail, all of whom possess night-pearls of a type not commercially available on the continental market. The University of Hornhold maintains a single such pearl in its curiosity cabinet, donated anonymously, which emits a faint bioluminescence that no alchemical analysis has been able to explain.
Mysterious Phenomena

The Felidae Mystery Across the entire continent, legends persist of elusive beings described as "mischievous catfolk hiding in shadows." Nearly every civilization has its own version of "the cats in the shadows" folklore, but the Concordat region has become the area with the most frequent and well-documented sightings over the past century. While often dismissed as superstition or children's tales, these stories show remarkable consistency: Ancient minotaur carvings in early Hornhold iterations depict humanoid figures with distinctly feline features. Deeproot folk tales describe "shadow cats who walk as people" helping lost children find their way home. Even kobold tribal myths include references to "the tall cats who taught the first mining techniques." Continental scholars are divided on the phenomenon, but the more comprehensive theories suggest a connection to shadow magic—specifically, the aspect that disrupts spatial continuity. Around 3E 1700, Lyjousturnur took a keen interest in this mystery and commissioned a detailed investigation by the Continental Mage Association and other institutions. This seven-year investigation left behind extensive records. Scholars from across the continent, applying the latest theories of shadow magic, conducted numerous experiments, primarily around Larkghet. However, their findings ultimately challenged the very theoretical foundations they were based on: out of 92 "confirmed" sightings meticulously documented during the investigation, only 6 occurred in the Larkghet area, with the vast majority scattered across larger settlements throughout the Concordat and beyond. The final report failed to produce a convincing theory to explain the phenomenon, concluding only that the manifestations appeared to be weakly correlated with areas of high population density or emotional resonance, rather than specific magical ley lines or spatial rifts as initially hypothesized. This outcome dealt a significant blow to contemporary shadow magic theory and left the Felidae Mystery as perplexing as ever.

The Singing Crystals of Ly's Peak Certain crystal formations deep within the Dragontooth Mountains emit harmonic tones when exposed to moonlight. Kobold shamans carve these crystals into ritual instruments believed to communicate with Helixus. A complete "crystal chorus"—a set of perfectly tuned singing crystals—is among the most valuable ritual objects in kobold society. Beyond their religious significance, some scholars and Coven practitioners believe Singing Crystals possess the ability to store and replay sounds when properly activated, functioning as a form of magical recording device. The kobolds neither confirm nor deny this claim, maintaining the crystals' sacred status. Unauthorized removal of these crystals from kobold territory is strictly forbidden, though black market specimens command extraordinary prices from collectors willing to risk kobold wrath and Concordat legal consequences.

The Temporal Pools Several small lakes in the high mountains are rumored to occasionally exhibit strange temporal properties. Objects or creatures that enter the water may emerge moments later having experienced years of subjective time, or vice versa—spending what feels like hours in the water only to discover mere seconds have passed in the outside world. Most scholars dismiss these as tall tales, but certain mountain communities maintain strict taboos about approaching these waters. The University of Hornhold keeps a sealed collection of objects allegedly recovered from these pools, including plants and minerals unknown to contemporary science—though whether these represent temporal anomalies or simply rare specimens from unexplored regions remains debated.

The Ghost Fleet of Garnetport On foggy nights during specific lunar phases, sailors report seeing spectral ships in Garnetport harbor—vessels lost during the Shimmerbay Calamity that never reached safety. These phantom ships supposedly carry valuable cargo and artifacts from Shimmerbay, but those who attempt to board them either return empty-handed or don't return at all. The Garnetport harbor master maintains an official registry of ghost ship sightings, mapping patterns that some treasure hunters use to predict future appearances. Skeptics note that sightings conveniently increase when fog obscures vision and when sailors have been drinking, suggesting natural explanations involving real ships glimpsed through mist or simple hallucination. The Star Maps of Whisperleaf Before their exodus, Whisperleaf elves reportedly created elaborate astronomical maps carved into living trees throughout the forest. These maps allegedly predict celestial events thousands of years in advance and identify cosmic alignments that enhance specific types of magic. The returning elven population has recovered some of this knowledge but believes many maps remain undiscovered in remote forest sections. Elven authorities carefully guard information about recovered maps, limiting access to trusted scholars and practitioners. What celestial knowledge these maps contain—and whether they truly possess predictive power or simply record historical observations—remains largely unknown to non-elven researchers.

The Kobold Gem-Speaking An ancient kobold technique for communicating across vast distances using specially prepared crystal pairs. When one crystal is spoken to, its paired crystal supposedly reproduces the exact sounds regardless of distance. This technology was allegedly used extensively during early kobold migrations but has been largely lost. Occasionally, miners discover matched crystal pairs that exhibit unusual resonance properties when separated—humming, vibrating, or producing faint sounds in response to activity near their partner. These discoveries fuel attempts to rediscover the lost art, with both the University of Hornhold and various Coven practitioners conducting experiments to recreate the effect. Kobold elders maintain cryptic silence about whether the technique truly existed or represents mythologized memory of more mundane communication methods. Their reticence may indicate the knowledge remains preserved in select shamanic lineages, or it may simply reflect uncertainty about whether their ancestors' capabilities matched the legends.
#notable settlements and locations
Major Settlements

Garnetport Urban Form and Geography Garnetport stands as the Concordat's largest city and its crown jewel—the settlement that most clearly embodies the region's transformation from a collection of isolated communities into a prosperous, unified realm under draconic protection. Its distinctive anvil-shaped layout reflects both its natural setting and centuries of organic growth. The Garnet River divides the city almost evenly into northern and southern halves, with nine bridges of varying sizes connecting the two banks. The largest and most impressive of these bridges carries The Garnet Way across the river, forming the city's central axis as the primary arterial route traverses from the northern bank through the heart of the urban core. The city's two major harbors occupy the indented sections of the anvil shape—the characteristic concave curves on either side of the anvil's body. North Port handles maritime commerce with the northwestern continent, the northern archipelago, and the eastern portions of the home continent. South Port manages trade with the southern kingdoms of the home continent and the western continental lands across distant seas. This division of harbor functions allows specialized facilities and merchant communities to develop around each port's particular trade patterns. Districts and Quarters The central axis along the Garnet Way hosts the Middle City's commercial heart and the city's primary temples. Its architecture reflects the diverse origins of Garnetport's population, blending styles brought by various refugee groups over the centuries into a distinctive cosmopolitan aesthetic. The district houses numerous guildhalls, including the Garnetport quarter of the Concordat Rangers, which maintains its headquarters here to facilitate coordination with merchant guilds and civic authorities. The Grand Bazaar, Garnetport's legendary marketplace, occupies a prime position at the anvil's center on the river's southern bank, directly facing the grand Temple of Mercuria on the northern bank—a symbolic arrangement emphasizing the connection between commerce and divine favor. The Founder's Hall, dedicated to Exodia, stands prominently in the commercial district, positioned to face the sea—a reminder of the refugee origins of Garnetport's founding population and the courage required to cross dangerous waters seeking shelter. The Dragonspire, a towering structure serving as both lighthouse and temple to Helixus, rises from a small island directly west of the city. Its beacon guides ships safely into harbor while its religious functions honor the draconic authority that makes the city's prosperity possible. The island location emphasizes the structure's dual purpose, visible to both seafarers and city residents. The Crystal Gardens, a public park designed by the Arcane Sage Luckas Hurraman and featuring crystalline structures reminiscent of Lyjousturnur's distinctive bodily growths, occupies a strategic position on the city's eastern side.The gardens serve as a crucial connector: running east-west, they link the Lower City with the Upper City; running north-south, they connect the Upper City with the Middle City. This multi-directional accessibility makes the gardens a popular gathering place for citizens from all social strata. The Upper City extends to the northeast, climbing the terraced slopes where the city's elite maintain their residences, enjoying both elevated positions and relative distance from the bustle of the ports. The southeastern quarter houses the University of Garnetport, administrative district, and the Mercurian Exchange, forming an intellectual and bureaucratic counterweight to the commercial districts. The Lower City sprawls across the anvil's protruding head and along both flanks of the anvil's body, housing the working population, artisan workshops, warehouses, and the less prestigious commercial establishments that support the ports' daily operations. University of Garnetport Established around 3E 1730 as part of the Concordat formalization process, the University of Garnetport represents a deliberate institutional investment in education and intellectual development. The timing of its founding—during the period when the Concordat's governmental structures were being standardized and formalized—reflects the leadership's recognition that a prosperous commercial realm required not just trade networks but also centers of learning to train administrators, merchants, diplomats, and professionals. Though younger than Hornhold's ancient university, Garnetport's institution has leveraged the city's maritime connections and commercial wealth to develop its own distinctive academic identity and areas of excellence. The university is organized into seven colleges: Maritime Sciences, Commerce and Finance, Diplomacy and Languages, Fine Arts, Natural Philosophy, Medicine, and History and Governance. Notably absent is any formal College of Magical Studies, reflecting Garnetport's historical restrictions on magical education following the necromancer disaster around 3E 1680. The university's location in the southeastern quarter places it adjacent to the Mercurian Exchange and administrative buildings, facilitating close connections between academic inquiry and practical commercial and governmental application. Many faculty members maintain dual roles as scholars and consultants to merchant houses or city officials. The institution has become particularly renowned for its work in maritime navigation, trade law, and diplomatic protocol—areas where Garnetport's international connections provide unparalleled practical resources for study and research. Population and Character Population: ~120,000. As the Concordat's largest city and primary gateway to the world, Garnetport exhibits remarkable cosmopolitanism. Refugees and their descendants from the Continental Decline form the majority population, but Shimmerbay survivors and their families occupy influential positions in trade, crafts, and municipal governance. Recent, especially within the past 120 year, immigrants from across the known world drawn by the prosper economy add further number and diversity, particularly in the port districts where multilingual commerce is the norm. The city's character reflects its commercial foundation—pragmatic, adaptable, and perpetually focused on opportunity. While other Concordat settlements maintain stronger connections to ancient traditions, Garnetport looks outward and forward, embracing innovation and change as necessary elements of prosperity.

Deeproot city Urban Form and Geography Deeproot's spindle-shaped layout—often described as fish-like by travelers—reflects its position at the confluence of two rivers. The Garnet River and Mistvein divide the settlement into three distinct sections: North City, South City, and the Eastern Sandbank. The Garnet Way passes through North City, connecting the settlement to both Garnetport downstream and New Hornhold upstream. However, South City serves as the nexus for southern and marsh connections: The Southern Way originates here, beginning its journey toward Aquilon and the southern territories, while The Marsh Path terminates here after its passage through Mistymarsh from Larkghet. Districts and Character South City, significantly larger than North City due to its role as the junction point for multiple trade routes, contains the famous Underground Market, established in the ancient water management systems built by the Water People and expanded over centuries. These subterranean halls provide cool, stable conditions ideal for certain goods and create a unique commercial environment that has become one of Deeproot's defining features. The district's surface level handles the agricultural commerce and river trade that form the economic foundation of the region. The importance of The Southern Way—carrying grain imports essential to Concordat food security and managing the flow of goods between the Concordat and its southern neighbors—has driven South City's development into Deeproot's commercial and administrative heart. The Deeproot quarter of the Concordat Rangers maintains its base here, positioned to respond to threats from the southern territories, the marshlands, and the surrounding countryside.The misty path also starts here towards the marshland. North City serves primarily as a transit zone for the Garnet Way traffic and houses much of the settlement's agricultural processing and storage facilities. The district's character reflects its function as an intersection point between different trade routes, though its economic activity remains secondary to South City's more diverse commercial life. The Eastern Sandbank, formed by river sediment deposits over millennia, hosts a fortress constructed by the "mountain people" in the post-Dwarf Kingdom era as a defensive response to expanding human powers from the south. This fortress now serves as Deeproot's administrative center, housing the council of regional elders and providing a defensible position should conflict ever threaten the settlement. Population and Character Adjacent to the fortress stands the Great Hall of Deeproot, originally constructed as a civic theater and assembly space. The Hall serves as the seat of the Concordat's four-chamber parliament during its formal sessions—convening two to three times per year, typically timed to coincide with the autumn grain trading season. When the parliament is not in session, the Hall reverts to its primary function as the region's largest public performance venue, hosting orcish storytelling traditions, minotaur historical reenactments, mountain people festivals, and southern theatrical productions in rotating seasons. The choice of Deeproot as parliamentary seat reflects the city's geographic centrality and political neutrality—a location where no faction is on home territory. Population: ~25,000. Deeproot's population primarily consists of "mountain people"(50%)—the mixed-blood descendants of humans, orcs, dwarves, and minotaurs who emerged during and after the Dwarf Kingdom's collapse. This demographic foundation creates a culture that values practical cooperation and adaptability over rigid ethnic or species loyalties. The settlement maintains stronger connections to traditional agricultural rhythms than either Garnetport or New Hornhold, though it has also developed sophisticated commercial practices through its role as a trade hub. The Underground Market particularly reflects this hybrid character, combining Water People engineering legacy with mountain people pragmatism and incorporating commercial practices from multiple cultural traditions.

New Hornhold City Historical Context and Urban Development The current iteration—the Third Hornhold—was established around 3E 1600, when minotaur leadership chose to rebuild not at the devastated Second Hornhold (Old Hornhold City) but at the site of the First Hornhold in the lower Garnet River valley. The First Hornhold had served as a forward fortress and trade post for over a millennium after the political center shifted to the Second Hornhold around 3E 200, and its surviving structures provided the foundation for the new city. The Arcane Sage Luckas Hurraman played a central role in this reconstruction, contributing architectural magic, structural reinforcement, and engineering expertise that gave the Third Hornhold a scale and sophistication minotaur engineering alone could not have achieved in so short a time. Rather than building an entirely new settlement, the reconstruction represented a re-urbanization of the old military stronghold, transforming it back into a thriving civic center. This process created the city's characteristic C-shaped expansion pattern, curving outward from the oldest fortified core. Urban Form and Geography New Hornhold stands on the north shore of Kronirr's Rest Lake, on the land between the Mazran River and the Garnet River, against the Garnet's west bank where the river enters the lake. Facing it across the Garnet is the university town, and far down the lake, where the Garnet flows out again, lies a small lakeside town. A bridge over the Garnet joins the city to the university town. West of the city a second bridge carries the roads over the Mazran. The lakeside town in the south has no bridge to either: it is reached by boat across the lake, or by the road around the western shore. The Fortresses and Key Districts Two fortresses from previous Hornhold iterations remain operational, one on each bank at the mouth of the Garnet. The larger fortress, on the east bank, houses the University of Hornhold, with its renowned Grand Archive, and the university town has grown around it. The smaller fortress, in the city, serves as the administrative center, where the Archon and advisory council conduct Concordat governance. The lakeside town at the lake's southern outlet, the settlement closest to Whisperleaf Forest, has become the primary location for elven commercial and economic activity. Elven merchants, scholars, and craftspeople maintain establishments here, creating a distinct cultural flavor that blends minotaur and elven traditions. The university town also serves as the launching point for eastern trade, with The Eastern Way beginning its journey from here toward Fort Alina and beyond. Its commercial facilities focus on goods moving to and from eastern kingdoms. The north gate is the city's main entrance for traffic from Old Hornhold City, with The Garnet Way's earliest segment entering here. The northern part of the city combines residential areas and commercial establishments serving local needs. The west gate is the city's western gateway, where The Garnet Way exits along the lakeshore and over the Mazran toward Deeproot and where The Dragon Way's western segment originates toward Windflow and the high mountains. The administrative fortress stands by the river mouth, surrounded by government offices, legal chambers, and the residences of officials and prominent citizens.
